newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-BSkyB year profit rises in Chisholm finale.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-BSkyB year profit rises in Chisholm finale.

text.p: British pay television group BSkyB Plc on Friday reported a 22 percent rise in pre-tax profit in its final year under the leadership of chief executive Sam Chisholm.

Feisty New Zealander Chisholm, who is stepping down in December after helping to make BSkyB one of the corporate success stories of the 1990s, signed off with pre-tax profit of 314 million pounds ($499.3 million) in the year to June 30.

The figure was boosted by a 14 million pound advance contribution on a programme supply deal. The underlying profit figure was at the bottom end of a narrow forecast range and BSkyB shares slipped 15 pence to 455p.
"Turnover and profits have grown strongly and debt levels have been reduced at a time when the company is investing for the future," Chisholm said in a statement.
"Our service now reaches one quarter of all homes in the UK and our subscribers are receiving more choice and better quality television than ever before," he added.

BSkyB said revenue should grow this year from higher subscription numbers and higher charges. But it added that programming and marketing costs would also rise as it prepares to launch a digital service next year.
BSkyB, a company 40 percent owned by Rupert Murdoch's News Corp, has seen its share price fall some 30 percent since February.

News that Chisholm and his deputy David Chance, both of whom have suffered health problems, were to step down undermined the stock. A further blow came when UK regulators forced BSkyB to withdraw from a UK digital terrestrial TV partnership with Carlton Communications Plc and Granada Group Plc.
BSkyB confirmed it was on course to launch 200-channel digital satellite TV in the UK next spring.

The move into the digital era will be led by Chisholm's successor Mark Booth, currently chief operating officer at News Corp's JSkyB venture in Japan. Chisholm and Chance will both remain as consultants and board members, while Murdoch's daughter Elisabeth is head of programming.

BSkyB has teamed up with British Telecom, Midland Bank and Japan's Matsushita to set up the British Interactive Broadcasting (BIB) venture to provide online services such as home shopping and banking for digital satellite customers.

A BIB subsidy will bring the retail cost of digital set-top boxes or decoders under 200 pounds. A decoder is required to view the new services, which BSkyB aims to deliver to homes via both satellite dishes and cable.
Chance told Reuters the box subsidy should mean that take-up was relatively rapid compared to slow starts experienced by operators in Germany and Italy.
"Coming in at 200 pounds will have a significant impact on relative take-up," he said.

Chance said BSkyB would offer near video on demand films on its new service. A film will be screened with staggered start-times so a viewer can sign up to watch it from the start at various stages of the evening. ($ = 0.628 British Pounds)
